safety.title: This is a risk state, not a five-minute technique
safety.body: Active suicidality needs your team, not a coached script. Route it, then build a plan collaboratively and supervised.
safety.note: Safety planning (Stanley-Brown) is collaborative, built with the patient and supervised — never generated here, and never a no-suicide 'contract' (no evidence; false reassurance).

frame.title: The bedside frame — five minutes, not fifty
frame.lead: You won't finish a course of therapy here. Read the mechanism driving today's crisis, match one brief technique, and hand the thread to outpatient care. No single school wins — fit beats brand (pooled SMD ~0.24, NNT ~7; CBT ≈ BA ≈ PST).
scaffold: 3 interventions: one skill, one activity, one connection
3 discharge tasks: appointment, means safety, warning-signs plan

cues.label: Keeps returning in crisis, overwhelmed by problems
Ambivalent about meds, treatment, or substance use
Confused or frightened by the illness itself

techniques.name: Behavioral Activation (micro-dose)

steps.t: Name the pattern out loud: “this looks like behavioral shutdown, not laziness.”
Pick ONE small, valued, doable-today activity with the patient (not a to-do list).
Make it concrete: what, when, with whom — schedule it into today.
Close the loop tomorrow: did it happen? how did mood shift? adjust.

scriptLines: “Depression makes everything feel pointless before you start — so we act first and let motivation catch up. What’s one small thing that used to matter to you?”
“Could we put a 10-minute walk after lunch on today’s plan, together?”
techniques.evidence: Superior to usual care for depression (SMD ~ −0.78), on par with CBT, and the lowest cognitive demand — the best inpatient fit for a shut-down patient.
techniques.caution: Keep it small and valued, not a chore list; failure to complete an over-ambitious plan reinforces hopelessness.
techniques.handoff: Note the chosen activity + response so outpatient can continue the activation schedule.

techniques.name: DBT distress tolerance — TIPP

steps.t: Validate first, then offer a skill: “this is a lot — want a way to bring the intensity down fast?”
Temperature: cool water on the face / cold pack to shift physiology.
Intense exercise (brief), Paced breathing (longer exhale), Paired muscle relaxation.
Reassess arousal; once the wave passes, debrief what helped.

scriptLines: “Your body is in alarm right now — let’s lower the alarm before we problem-solve.”
“Breathe out slower than you breathe in — I’ll count with you.”
techniques.evidence: Skills-containing DBT arms outperform for self-injury in dismantling trials.
techniques.caution: A distress-tolerance skill is for riding out a wave — not a substitute for a safety assessment when risk is present.
techniques.handoff: Note which skill helped so it can be rehearsed and carried to outpatient DBT.

techniques.name: Chain analysis (after an incident)

steps.t: Non-punitive stance: “let’s understand what happened, together — not to judge it.”
Walk the sequence: vulnerability → trigger → thoughts/feelings → action → consequences.
Find the function the behavior served (escape, communication, relief).
Identify one earlier link where a skill could change the chain next time.

scriptLines: “Take me back to right before it happened — what was going on?”
“What did it do for you in that moment? What did it cost afterward?”
techniques.evidence: Turns an incident into a formulation and a plan; a core DBT move that replaces a punitive response.
techniques.caution: Do it collaboratively and non-judgmentally; a blaming tone re-traumatizes and shuts down disclosure.
techniques.handoff: Document the chain + the identified skill-insertion point for the outpatient therapist.

techniques.name: Problem-Solving Therapy (4-step micro-session)

steps.t: Define ONE concrete, solvable problem (not the whole life).
Brainstorm options without judging them yet.
Choose one workable option together (pros/cons quickly).
Plan the first small step and when it happens.

scriptLines: “There’s a lot going on — if we could solve just one piece this week, which would help most?”
“Let’s list options first; we’ll pick after — no bad ideas yet.”
techniques.evidence: Reduces repeat self-harm re-presentation (13.5% vs 22.1%, NNT 12).
techniques.caution: Keep the problem bounded; an unbounded problem defeats the method and deepens overwhelm.
techniques.handoff: Note the defined problem + chosen step so outpatient can continue the format.

techniques.name: Motivational Interviewing (brief)

steps.t: Roll with resistance — don’t argue the change side; that entrenches it.
Ask open questions; reflect and affirm autonomy.
Evoke change talk: “what would be different if…?”, importance/confidence rulers (0–10).
Summarize the patient’s own reasons; ask permission before advising.

scriptLines: “On a scale of 0–10, how important is cutting back right now? … Why not a lower number?”
“You get to decide — what do you make of all this?”
techniques.evidence: Improves engagement and substance-use outcomes; pairs with the Motivational Interviewing page.
techniques.caution: The righting reflex (persuading, warning) predictably increases sustain talk — resist it.
techniques.handoff: Note the patient’s stated reasons + readiness so outpatient can build on the change talk.

techniques.name: Psychoeducation (as a conversation)

steps.t: Ask what they already understand and fear about the illness.
Offer a simple, non-stigmatizing illness model in their words.
Build a warning-signs / early-action plan together.
Loop in family when possible — with the patient’s permission.

scriptLines: “What’s your understanding of what’s been happening to you?”
“What are the earliest signs, for you, that things are slipping — and what could we do then?”
techniques.evidence: The strongest single inpatient psychological intervention: readmission NNT ~5, relapse NNT ~9.
techniques.caution: A conversation, not a packet dump; check understanding rather than lecturing.
techniques.handoff: Share the warning-signs plan + family involvement status with outpatient.
